title: Entropy fall under reversible symbol expansion disappears per source character and is matched by padding (4 languages x 3 codebooks)
statement: Computed on 60,000 words of the pinned Latin reference text (vs.facts.ref_words('latin')), lower-cased, words joined by spaces. H1 = single-symbol entropy, H2 = conditional entropy of a symbol given the previous one (Bennett's second-order), both in bits. Encodings: (a) a random letter substitution; (b) a reversible verbose code mapping each letter to a fixed distinct pair drawn from 12 new symbols (space kept), length x1.84; (c) padding: a fixed null symbol after every letter, same length x1.84. Results, per output character / per source character (H2 x length ratio): source H2 3.358 / 3.358; substitution 3.358 / 3.358; verbose H1 3.495, H2 2.528 / 4.660; padding H1 3.139, H2 2.097 / 3.866. So (1) normalised by the length of the original source the fall does not persist: per source character the second-order entropy rises under both expansions, because a one-symbol context covers half a source letter; (2) against a matched padding control the verbose fall is not unusual: padding, which adds no information and encodes nothing, lowers per-character H2 further (2.10) than the verbose code (2.53). A low per-glyph H2 in the manuscript therefore cannot by itself point to a verbose cipher over a meaningless or a padded text; any claim needs the per-source-unit comparison and a padding control at the same expansion. Replication across four reference languages and three random codebooks each (H2 per output character / per source character): latin    source 3.36 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.53/4.66 2.47/4.56 2.50/4.61 | padding 2.10/3.87; italian  source 3.12 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.44/4.41 2.47/4.47 2.47/4.47 | padding 2.08/3.76; german   source 3.06 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.50/4.53 2.45/4.44 2.42/4.39 | padding 2.07/3.76; english  source 3.29 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.58/4.67 2.59/4.68 2.53/4.57 | padding 2.16/3.91. Every codebook in every language shows the same pattern: per-character H2 falls by about 0.6-0.8 bits, per-source-character H2 rises by about 1.2-1.4 bits, and padding lowers per-character H2 about 0.4 bits more than the verbose code. This is stable enough to register as a fact about the measure, not about the manuscript.
check: recompute H1/H2 for the four encodings on vs.facts.ref_words('latin', 60000) with the stated constructions; per-source normalisation = H2 x (output length / source length)
